title: How to Meet Muslim Singles in Toronto (A Guide From Someone Who Was Very Bad At It)
summary: Wondering how to meet Muslim singles in Toronto? Here’s what I learned from mosques, Muslim events, aunties, talking stages, & finally Muzz.
body_markdown:
For two years I was convinced Toronto had run out of single Muslims. Not “dating pool feels small” convinced — actually convinced, like the city had quietly relocated all of them somewhere I wasn’t invited. I’d sit on my bed at 11pm doing the kind of spiral math you do when you’re lonely and bored: how many Muslims even live here, how many of them are my age, how many of those are single, how many of those would I actually get along with. The number always ended up depressingly close to zero.


It wasn’t zero. It was never zero. I was just looking for one person in a city, when I should’ve been looking for one person in a system.


### **The Part Where I Was Wrong About the Numbers**


### Looking for your soulmate?


You won’t find your soulmate on this blog post but you might find them on Muzz - the world’s biggest Muslim dating and marriage app.

Here’s the thing nobody tells you: there are north of 400,000 Muslims in the Greater Toronto Area. That’s not a rounding error, that’s close to 10% of the entire metro population, and Ontario has the highest share of Muslims of any province in the country. In Mississauga—Erin Mills, more than a quarter of the neighbourhood is Muslim. Same story in Milton. Same story in pockets of Don Valley you’d never guess unless you actually lived there.


So no, the pool was never the problem. I was standing in Thorncliffe Park thinking about someone who, statistically, was probably in Milton. Toronto Muslims aren’t one neighbourhood — we’re Thorncliffe Park and Flemingdon Park, we’re Etobicoke where Jami Mosque has stood since 1968 with the oldest Ottoman-style minaret in Ontario, we’re Scarborough, North York, Mississauga, Milton. That spread means the community is genuinely massive. It also means the single Muslim two postal codes over might as well not exist to you, because you’re never going to bump into them at the grocery store. Your five closest friends already know everyone in their own five-friend radius. That’s the actual bottleneck. Not scarcity. Geography, and a social circle too small to cover a city this size.


### **Where I Actually Looked (And Why Most of It Didn’t Work — Not Because It Was Wrong, Just Incomplete)**


I did the things you’re supposed to do. I showed up to Jummah more consistently than my iman alone would’ve gotten me there, not gonna lie. I went to iftars. When the Islamic Society of Toronto opened that huge new masjid in Thorncliffe Park, I was there the first week, half for the du’a and half hoping to casually make eye contact with my future spouse across the prayer hall like this was a movie. It wasn’t a movie. Nobody’s at Jummah trying to get set up, and honestly, that’s not what a mosque is for — but being in those rooms regularly still matters. A lot of people’s friend group, and eventually their spouse’s friend group, traces back to showing up somewhere on purpose.


I went to MuslimFest at Mississauga Celebration Square — genuinely one of the best weekends of my year, food and comedy and thousands of people, zero dating pressure, which also means zero dating results unless you’re bold enough to just talk to a stranger between the samosa line and the mainstage. I did Halal Bites Festival. I did the auntie thing — my mom’s friend set me up with four different guys over two years, each one a perfectly nice person who was in absolutely no way compatible with me, because one auntie’s network tops out at a few dozen people and I needed a pool of hundreds of thousands.


And I did the talking stage thing, more than once. Matched with someone through a mutual friend, talked for eight months, said things like “let’s see where it goes,” and it went nowhere, because neither of us had actually said out loud what we wanted. Inshallah is not a strategy. I learned that one the hard way, twice.


### **Tie Your Camel First**


There’s a hadith I heard a hundred times growing up and only actually understood at maybe year one and a half of being single in this city: a man asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he should tie his camel and trust in Allah, or just trust in Allah and leave it untied. The answer was — tie your camel, then trust in Allah.


I had the trust part down. I prayed about it, I made du’a, I told myself inshallah it’ll happen when it’s meant to happen. What I wasn’t doing was tying the camel. I was waiting for the right person to wander into my five-friend radius instead of actually widening the radius. Showing up to Jummah is good. Going to MuslimFest is good. But if that’s the whole plan, you’re leaving the camel untied and calling it faith.


Tying the camel, for me, ended up meaning something pretty unglamorous: I went to one of the in-person Muslim singles events Muzz runs in Toronto — a few hundred people, no pressure, everyone already opted in — and I put myself properly on the app in between. Not as a backup plan. As the actual plan. Because an app doesn’t care whether you’re in Thorncliffe Park or Erin Mills or Milton — it puts the whole GTA in front of you at once, filtered by the stuff that actually matters, instead of by who happens to live near you or who your auntie already knows.


### **And Then, Annoyingly, It Just Happened**


I’d love to tell you there was a lightning-bolt moment. There wasn’t. I matched with someone on Muzz who’d also been to that same singles event and somehow we’d missed each other in the room. We talked for three weeks, not eight months, because we’d both gotten tired enough of the talking stage to just say what we actually wanted early. First date was at a halal spot neither of us had heard of, which is its own kind of Toronto Muslim rite of passage.


I’m not saying an app is romantic. It isn’t. Neither is a spreadsheet, and dating in a city this size is basically a spreadsheet problem wearing a trench coat. What I’m saying is: the community is here, all 400,000-plus of us, spread across a metro area too big for any one auntie or any one Jummah to cover on its own. Go to MuslimFest. Show up to Jummah. Let your auntie try, honestly, she means well. But also tie the camel — put yourself somewhere that actually reaches the whole city, not just your corner of it.


You’re not the only one still looking. You were just looking in a five-friend radius, in a city built for hundreds of thousands.
